kurals.tamil:
அன்பின் விழையார் பொருள்விழையும் ஆய்தொடியார்
இன்சொல் இழுக்குத் தரும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Anbin vizhaiyaar porulvizhaiyum aaydhodiyaar
insol izhukkuth tharum.
kurals.meaning: The sweet words of bangle-adorned women who want a man not out of love but for his money will in the end bring him disgrace and grief.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a kid who suddenly calls you their best friend every day you bring a big bag of candy, and ignores you on days you bring nothing. Their nice words feel good, but they were never about you, and trusting them only ends with hurt feelings. Real friendship is liking someone, not liking what they can give you.
kurals.university: The opening couplet sets the chapter’s key contrast between anbu (அன்பு, love) and porul (பொருள், wealth): the women described here vizhaiyaar, ‘do not desire’, out of love but porul-vizhaiyum, ‘desire wealth’. Aaydhodiyaar (ஆய்தொடியார், ‘those wearing choice bangles’) is a conventional ornamental epithet, and the danger lies in their insol (இன்சொல், sweet speech), the same virtue Valluvar praises in chapter 10, here turned into a tool of profit. Izhukku (இழுக்கு) means both moral lapse and resulting disgrace; Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah render it as ‘suffering’, Sivayogi Sivakumar as ‘degradation’. Parimelazhagar places the chapter in the Natpiyal (section on friendship) right after Penvazhicheral (being led by one’s wife), and reads it as a warning against an intimacy that only imitates friendship. The text is identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Happiness is said to be in the mode of passion when it is derived from the contact of the senses with their objects. Such happiness is like nectar at first but poison at the end.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes rajasic pleasure as sweet at the start and bitter at the end.
hinduism.tie_back: The insincere sweet words of Kural 911 are nectar at first, and the izhukku they bring is the poison at the end.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong match on the sweet-then-bitter pattern; the Gita speaks of sense pleasure in general, not hired affection.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For they that are such serve not our Lord Jesus Christ, but their own belly; and by good words and fair speeches deceive the hearts of the simple.”
christianity.explanation: Paul warns about people who use pleasant language to deceive the naive while serving only their own appetite.
christianity.tie_back: Same picture as the Kural: fair speech covering pure self-interest.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close on sweet-but-self-serving speech; Paul’s target is false teachers, not mercenary lovers.

islam.quote_or_event: “And when you see them, their forms please you, and if they speak, you listen to their speech. [They are] as if they were pieces of wood propped up...”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes hypocrites whose looks and words are attractive but who are hollow inside.
islam.tie_back: Like the women of Kural 911, they please the eye and ear while having no real heart for you.
islam._accuracy_note: Good fit on attractive speech hiding emptiness, but the verse is about religious hypocrites.

judaism.quote_or_event: “All love that depends on a something, [when the] thing ceases, [the] love ceases; and [all love] that does not depend on anything, will never cease.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah separates love that depends on some benefit from love that stands on its own, and says the first ends when the benefit ends.
judaism.tie_back: Valluvar’s women love the porul, not the person, which is exactly the love that ‘depends on a something’.
judaism._accuracy_note: Near-identical principle: conditional love versus unconditional love.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Among the ‘foes in the guise of friends’, the Buddha lists the one who renders lip-service, who among other things “tries to gain one’s favor by empty words.”
buddhism.explanation: The Sigalovada Sutta teaches a layman to recognize false friends whose kind words have no substance behind them.
buddhism.tie_back: Kural 911’s insol is the same kind of empty, favor-seeking speech.
buddhism._accuracy_note: The quoted phrase is verbatim; the sutta speaks of false friends generally.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Hesiod’s myth of Pandora, the gods dress the first woman in beauty and grace, and Hermes puts lies, crafty words and a deceitful nature in her heart, so that she becomes a lovely gift that brings men trouble.
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod’s story is about a beautiful surface hiding deceit and harm.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Kural 911 likewise warns of an adorned figure whose sweet words bring ruin.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Thematic match on adorned deceit; Hesiod blames womankind as a whole, which Valluvar does not, so the parallel is partial.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Therefore those who love for the sake of utility love for the sake of what is good for themselves... and not in so far as the other is the person loved but in so far as he is useful or pleasant.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle says friendships of utility are not really about the other person but about what one gets.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the porul-vizhaiyum (wealth-desiring) affection of Kural 911, described as philosophy.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VIII.3 (tr. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong conceptual match on affection that is really self-interest.

kurals.tamil:
பயன்தூக்கிப் பண்புரைக்கும் பண்பின் மகளிர்
நயன்தூக்கி நள்ளா விடல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Payandhookkip panburaikkum panbin magalir
nayandhookki nallaa vidal.
kurals.meaning: Weigh carefully the conduct of characterless women who first measure what they can gain from a man and then talk sweetly of virtue, and keep away from them.
kurals.elementary: Some people check how much pocket money you have before deciding how friendly to be, and then talk about how loyal they are. Valluvar says: notice that pattern, think about it, and do not get close to someone who measures you by your wallet.
kurals.university: The couplet rests on a play of the verb thookku (தூக்கு, ‘to weigh, to measure’): the women payan-thookki, ‘weigh the profit’, so the wise man must nayan-thookki, ‘weigh their character’, and then nallaa vidal (நள்ளா விடல்), ‘leave without joining’. There is also deliberate irony in panburaikkum panbin magalir, ‘women of no virtue (panbu) who speak of virtue’: the speech is a performance tuned to the size of the purse. Puliyur Kesigan reads nayan as their behaviour, while Mu. Varadarasanar takes it as the ‘pleasure’ they offer, which the wise man evaluates and declines. Parimelazhagar treats the couplet as a practical rule of discernment rather than a moral sermon, in keeping with the Porutpal’s concern with prudent conduct. No textual variants appear between ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Kathasaritsagara’s tale of Lohajangha, the courtesan Rupinika’s mother Makaradamshtra drives away the penniless young man her daughter genuinely loves, insisting that affection must follow money; the story then shows how calculation and greed undo themselves.
hinduism.explanation: Somadeva’s story collection uses this tale to satirize affection that is weighed against wealth.
hinduism.tie_back: Makaradamshtra is a portrait of payan-thookki, weighing the gain before the man.
hinduism.source: Somadeva, Kathasaritsagara, Book II (tale of Lohajangha), tr. C. H. Tawney
hinduism._accuracy_note: The plot is summarized from the standard Tawney translation but could not be re-checked live this session, so it is scored cautiously.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And when he had spent all, there arose a mighty famine in that land; and he began to be in want.”
christianity.explanation: In the parable of the Prodigal Son, the companions of the young man’s wasteful days disappear once his money is gone; the story adds that ‘no man gave unto him’.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s mercenary friends likewise last only as long as the purse does.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verse 14 is quoted verbatim; the link to mercenary affection is narrative, not stated.

islam.quote_or_event: “And of the people is he whose speech pleases you in worldly life, and he calls Allah to witness as to what is in his heart, yet he is the fiercest of opponents.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an warns of people who speak pleasantly and even swear to their sincerity while being enemies at heart.
islam.tie_back: Kural 912’s women ‘speak of virtue’ while weighing gain, the same gap between pleasing words and real intent.
islam._accuracy_note: Matches calculated, pleasing speech that hides a contrary heart; the context is political and religious.

judaism.quote_or_event: “With her much fair speech she causeth him to yield, With the blandishment of her lips she enticeth him away.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs describes the enticing woman whose skilled talk leads a simple young man astray.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts warn against flattering speech that is a means to an end.
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close on calculated, enticing speech; Proverbs does not stress the money motive here.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “One is a bottle friend; one says, ‘friend, friend’ only to one’s face; one is a friend and an associate only when it is advantageous.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes people whose friendship lasts only while there is something in it for them.
buddhism.tie_back: Exactly the friendship Kural 912 says to weigh and walk away from.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Eriphyle, wife of the seer Amphiaraus, was bribed by Polynices with the golden necklace of Harmonia and in return persuaded her husband to join the doomed expedition against Thebes, where he died.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth became the Greek byword for affection and loyalty sold for a jewel.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Eriphyle weighs gold against the man, as the women of Kural 912 weigh profit before speaking.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good emblem of affection sold for gold, but Eriphyle is a wife, not a courtesan.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “...there is a dishonour in being overcome by the love of money, or of wealth, or of political power... For none of these things are of a permanent or lasting nature; not to mention that no generous friendship ever sprang from them.”
philosophy.explanation: Pausanias’ speech holds that attachments bought by money are shameful and cannot produce real friendship.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar likewise tells the wise to weigh such attachments and refuse them.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verbatim from Jowett; very close on the point that wealth-based attachment cannot be genuine.

kurals.tamil:
பொருட்பெண்டிர் பொய்ம்மை முயக்கம் இருட்டறையில்
ஏதில் பிணந்தழீஇ அற்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Porutpendir poimmai muyakkam iruttaraiyil
edhil pinandhazheei atru.
kurals.meaning: The false embrace of women who want only money is like hugging a stranger’s corpse in a dark room: there is no warmth or feeling in it at all.
kurals.elementary: Think of hugging a big cardboard cut-out of a friend in the dark. It is shaped like a person, but nobody is really there to hug you back. Valluvar says that affection bought with money is like that: it looks like love, but there is no real heart inside it.
kurals.university: Kural 913 is the chapter’s most startling simile. Porut-pendir (பொருட்பெண்டிர், ‘women of wealth’, i.e. women who are for wealth) offer a poimmai muyakkam (பொய்ம்மை முயக்கம், false embrace), compared to clasping an edhil pinam (ஏதில் பிணம், a stranger’s corpse) in an iruttarai (இருட்டறை, dark room). Parimelazhagar’s gloss, followed by Puliyur Kesigan and by the bracketed ‘(hired men)’ in the standard English explanation, explains the image: it is the hired corpse-bearer who handles an unknown body in the dark for pay, without any bond, so the transaction is equally loveless on both sides. Kalaignar reads it as acting out love purely for money. The form thazheei (தழீஇ) is an alapedai (lengthened vowel) form of thazhuvi, ‘having embraced’. Both base sources agree on the text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The pleasures that arise from contact with the sense objects, though appearing as enjoyable to worldly-minded people, are verily a source of misery... so the wise do not delight in them.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that pleasures born only of sense contact are empty and end in sorrow.
hinduism.tie_back: Kural 913 shows the same emptiness in its most vivid form: an embrace with no living heart in it.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Shares the theme of hollow sense pleasure; lacks the Kural’s corpse image.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Then when lust hath conceived, it bringeth forth sin: and sin, when it is finished, bringeth forth death.”
christianity.explanation: James traces a path from desire to sin to death.
christianity.tie_back: Valluvar puts death at the very center of the embrace itself, which is cold as a corpse.
christianity._accuracy_note: Links desire and death, but as moral consequence rather than a picture of loveless contact.

islam.quote_or_event: “But those who disbelieved - their deeds are like a mirage in a lowland which a thirsty one thinks is water until, when he comes to it, he finds it is nothing...”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an compares empty deeds to a mirage that promises water and gives nothing.
islam.tie_back: The false embrace in Kural 913 also looks like love up close and turns out to hold nothing.
islam._accuracy_note: Shared image of an empty promise; the Qur’anic context is about unbelief.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Her house is the way to the nether-world, Going down to the chambers of death.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs ends its warning about the enticing woman by linking her house to death.
judaism.tie_back: Kural 913 also ties this intimacy to death, through the corpse in the dark room.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong shared link between such intimacy and death and darkness; the images differ.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Behold this body — a painted image, a mass of heaped up sores, infirm, full of hankering — of which nothing is lasting or stable!”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada asks the reader to see the attractive body as a painted surface over decay.
buddhism.tie_back: Valluvar likewise strips the purchased embrace down to what it really is: a lifeless body.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Both use bodily, corpse-like images to break infatuation; the Buddhist point is impermanence, not insincerity.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Underworld, Odysseus tries three times to embrace the shade of his mother Anticleia, and three times she slips through his arms like a shadow or a dream.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer’s scene shows an embrace that holds nothing living.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Kural 913’s embrace of a corpse is also contact without any real presence, though Homer’s scene is tender rather than mercenary.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Only the image of an empty embrace is shared; the emotional context is the opposite.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle argues that self-indulgence in the pleasures of touch is especially open to reproach because it belongs to us not as human beings but as animals.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, pleasure cut off from reason and relationship is the least human kind.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar’s corpse simile makes the same point more harshly: a purely bought embrace has nothing human in it.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased, not re-checked live this session; a reasonable but loose thematic parallel.

kurals.tamil:
பொருட்பொருளார் புன்னலந் தோயார் அருட்பொருள்
ஆயும் அறிவி னவர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Porutporulaar punnalan thoyaar arutporul
aayum arivi navar.
kurals.meaning: People of wisdom, who seek the true wealth of grace and compassion, will not touch the cheap charms of those for whom money is the only thing that matters.
kurals.elementary: If you are saving up for something really valuable, like a bicycle, you do not spend it all on sweets that are gone in a minute. Wise people treat their hearts the same way: they look for real kindness, not for ‘friendships’ that are only about money.
kurals.university: The couplet turns on a pun on porul: porut-porulaar (பொருட்பொருளார்) are ‘those whose object (porul) is wealth (porul)’, set against arut-porul (அருட்பொருள்), ‘the wealth that is arul (grace, compassion)’, which the wise aayum (ஆயும், examine and pursue). Punnalam (புன்னலம், ‘petty or base beauty’) is the low pleasure they decline, and thoyaar (தோயார்) means ‘will not immerse themselves in or touch’. Mu. Varadarasanar treats arul itself as the highest wealth, while Solomon Pappaiah reads arut-porul as ‘wealth sought together with compassion’, a reading in keeping with Parimelazhagar’s concern that riches be earned and used with arul. The echo of chapter 25 (Aruludaimai) is deliberate. Ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net agree, with punnalan(th) sandhi spelled புன்னலந்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Katha Upanishad, Yama teaches Nachiketas that the good (shreyas) and the pleasant (preyas) both come to a person; the wise examine them and choose the good, while the foolish choose the pleasant for the sake of getting and keeping.
hinduism.explanation: The Upanishad says real wisdom is discerning lasting good from passing pleasure.
hinduism.tie_back: The aayum arivinar of Kural 914 are exactly those who examine and choose shreyas (arut-porul) over preyas (punnalam).
hinduism._accuracy_note: Close structural match: discerning wisdom choosing the higher good; paraphrased.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt... But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven...”
christianity.explanation: Jesus contrasts perishable earthly wealth with lasting spiritual treasure.
christianity.tie_back: Valluvar’s wise man prefers arut-porul, the wealth of grace, to the petty pleasures money can buy.
christianity._accuracy_note: Clear match on ranking spiritual wealth above material wealth.

islam.quote_or_event: “Wealth and children are [but] adornment of the worldly life. But the enduring good deeds are better to your Lord for reward and better for [one's] hope.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an ranks lasting righteous deeds above worldly adornments.
islam.tie_back: The same choice of lasting good (arut-porul) over passing charm runs through Kural 914.
islam._accuracy_note: Good match on the higher wealth; the Qur’an does not address hired affection here.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Who is rich? He who rejoices in his lot...”
judaism.explanation: Ben Zoma redefines wealth as contentment rather than possessions.
judaism.tie_back: Like Valluvar, the Mishnah moves true wealth from money to an inner good.
judaism._accuracy_note: Shares the redefinition of wealth; contentment is not the same as arul (compassion).

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Riches ruin only the foolish, not those in quest of the Beyond. By craving for riches the witless man ruins himself as well as others.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says wealth harms only those who crave it, not those seeking the higher goal.
buddhism.tie_back: In Kural 914 the money-minded ruin themselves, while the seekers of arul stay untouched.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Shares the split between wealth-cravers and seekers of the higher good.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At a crossroads the young Heracles meets two women: Vice, who promises an easy road of pleasures, and Virtue, who offers a harder road to lasting honor; he chooses Virtue.
greek_mythology.explanation: Prodicus’ fable, retold by Xenophon, became the classic Greek picture of a moral choice.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Kural 914’s wise man makes the same choice, turning from punnalam toward arut-porul.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong match on the wise choice of a higher good over seductive pleasure; paraphrased.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In his defense speech, Socrates says his whole mission was to persuade Athenians, young and old, not to care first for their bodies or property but for the greatest improvement of the soul.
philosophy.explanation: Socrates ranks the soul’s good above wealth and bodily comfort.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar’s aayum arivinar likewise put the soul’s wealth, arul, above money-bought pleasure.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Good fit on the ranking of goods; paraphrased.

kurals.tamil:
பொதுநலத்தார் புன்னலம் தோயார் மதிநலத்தின்
மாண்ட அறிவி னவர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Podhunalaththaar punnalam thoyaar madhinalaththin
maanda arivi navar.
kurals.meaning: Those whose understanding has been perfected by good natural sense will not seek the low pleasures of women whose favors are offered to anyone who pays.
kurals.elementary: A smart kid who knows what real friendship is will not chase someone who is ‘best friends’ with whoever gives the most presents that day. Good sense helps you see that kind of friendship is not really for you at all.
kurals.university: Podhu-nalaththaar (பொதுநலத்தார்) means ‘those whose charms (nalam) are common (podhu)’, available to all who pay. Valluvar sets this against mathi-nalam (மதிநலம்), ‘the excellence of natural intelligence’, which makes knowledge maandu (மாண்ட, perfected, excellent). Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesigan distinguish iyarkai arivu (inborn sense) from acquired learning, and Kalaignar explicitly names both ‘natural intelligence and learned knowledge’, following Parimelazhagar’s distinction between mathi (native wit) and arivu (learning). The couplet is built parallel to 914 (punnalam thoyaar repeats), so the pair should be read together: 914 names the motive of the wise (arul), 915 the faculty (mathi). Both base sources give the same text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One who is able to withdraw the senses from their objects, just as a tortoise withdraws its limbs into its shell, is established in divine wisdom.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes the steady-minded person who can pull the senses back from their objects.
hinduism.tie_back: Valluvar’s person of perfected understanding likewise draws back from common, purchased pleasure.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Good match on wisdom showing itself as sense restraint; general rather than specific.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Flee also youthful lusts: but follow righteousness, faith, charity, peace, with them that call on the Lord out of a pure heart.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells Timothy to turn away from youthful passions and pursue virtue.
christianity.tie_back: The wise of Kural 915 likewise turn from low pleasure toward what is excellent.
christianity._accuracy_note: Fits the call to avoid; lacks the Kural’s emphasis on intelligence as the reason.

islam.quote_or_event: “Beautified for people is the love of that which they desire - of women and sons, heaped-up sums of gold and silver... That is the enjoyment of worldly life, but Allah has with Him the best return.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an notes that worldly desires are made attractive, but that a better return lies with God.
islam.tie_back: Kural 915’s wise man sees past what is made attractive, toward what is truly better.
islam._accuracy_note: Broad theme of attractive worldly desire versus a higher good; not specific to hired favors.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Lust not after her beauty in thy heart; Neither let her captivate thee with her eyelids.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs warns the young man not to let outward beauty capture him, and adds that such a woman reduces a man to a loaf of bread.
judaism.tie_back: Valluvar likewise tells the wise not to sink into podhu-nalam, beauty offered to all.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close match: a warning against being captured by hired beauty, with loss of wealth in the next verse.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Weeds are the bane of fields, lust is the bane of mankind. Therefore, what is offered to those free of lust yields abundant fruit.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada compares lust to weeds choking a field.
buddhism.tie_back: Valluvar’s wise keep their field clear by refusing common, purchased pleasure.
buddhism._accuracy_note: General teaching on lust; does not stress intelligence or the ‘common’ quality the Kural names.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Odysseus, held for years by the nymph Calypso, refuses her offer to make him immortal and ageless, choosing instead to return home to Ithaca and Penelope.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer shows his hero choosing what is truly his own over an easy, enchanting comfort.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Kural 915’s discerning man likewise refuses tempting pleasure in favor of what his good sense values.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Weak match: Calypso is not mercenary, and Homer stresses longing for home more than wisdom.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The Love who is the offspring of the common Aphrodite is essentially common, and has no discrimination, being such as the meaner sort of men feel...”
philosophy.explanation: Pausanias separates common (Pandemos) love, which is indiscriminate and bodily, from heavenly love, which looks to the soul.
philosophy.tie_back: Plato’s ‘common’ love echoes Valluvar’s podhu-nalam, and both say the wise prefer the higher kind.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verbatim from Jowett; strikingly close, even sharing the idea of ‘common’ love.

kurals.tamil:
தந்நலம் பாரிப்பார் தோயார் தகைசெருக்கிப்
புன்னலம் பாரிப்பார் தோள்.
kurals.transliteration:
Thannalam paarippaar thoyaar thagaiserukkip
punnalam paarippaar thol.
kurals.meaning: Those who care about their own good name will not seek the arms of women who, proud of their charm, offer their cheap favors to all who pay.
kurals.elementary: If you care about being known as honest and kind, you will be careful about who you spend your time with. You would not team up with someone who sells their ‘friendship’ to anyone, because you value your good name.
kurals.university: The couplet repeats the verb paarippaar (பாரிப்பார்) in two senses: those who paarippaar thannalam, ‘cherish or spread their own goodness (or fame)’, will not touch the shoulders of those who paarippaar punnalam, ‘spread their petty charms abroad’. Thagai-serukki (தகைசெருக்கி) is ‘being proud of their attractiveness or skill’. Solomon Pappaiah and Puliyur Kesigan take thannalam as one’s own fame, Mu. Varadarasanar as one’s ‘good conduct’, and Parimelazhagar as the reputation that comes from virtue. Textual note: thirukkural.net prints the first verb as பாரப்பார் (paarappaar), whereas ytamizh.com and the standard Parimelazhagar text read பாரிப்பார்; the repeated verb and all four commentaries support பாரிப்பார், so the variant looks like a typographical slip.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Elevate yourself through the power of your mind, and not degrade yourself, for the mind can be the friend and also the enemy of the self.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna places the responsibility for one’s rise or fall on oneself.
hinduism.tie_back: Kural 916’s thannalam paarippaar are those who choose to raise themselves and not to lower their own worth.
hinduism._accuracy_note: General self-respect principle; does not mention reputation or this temptation.

christianity.quote_or_event: “A good name is rather to be chosen than great riches, and loving favour rather than silver and gold.”
christianity.tie_back: Those who guard their thannalam (good name) in Kural 916 make exactly this choice.
christianity._accuracy_note: Matches the value placed on a good name; not about this specific temptation.

islam.quote_or_event: In Surah Yusuf, the wife of al-Aziz tries to seduce the young Joseph behind closed doors; he refuses, seeking refuge in God and saying he will not betray his master’s trust, and he flees.
islam.explanation: Yusuf’s refusal is the Qur’an’s model of a person who guards his integrity under pressure.
islam.tie_back: He is the type of the thannalam paarippaar who will not touch what would stain him.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong model of guarding one’s integrity; the temptress in the story is not mercenary.

judaism.quote_or_event: When Potiphar’s wife urges Joseph to be with her, he refuses, asking how he could do such a great wickedness and sin against God, and when she seizes his garment he leaves it and flees.
judaism.explanation: Genesis presents Joseph as the young man who protects his integrity even at personal cost.
judaism.tie_back: Joseph embodies Kural 916: one who values his own goodness does not take what is offered.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong example of self-respecting refusal; paraphrased.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Not to be contented with one's own wife, and to be seen with harlots and the wives of others — this is a cause of one's downfall.”
buddhism.explanation: The Parabhava Sutta lists such conduct among the causes of a person’s decline.
buddhism.tie_back: Kural 916 states the positive side: those who protect their standing stay away.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Direct match on avoidance as protection of one’s standing.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Queen Anteia tries to win the young hero Bellerophon, but he refuses her because he is upright of heart; in revenge she falsely accuses him to her husband.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer presents Bellerophon as the noble-minded young man who would not compromise his honor.
greek_mythology.tie_back: He is an early Greek picture of the thannalam paarippaar of Kural 916.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good emblem of honor-guarding refusal; Anteia is not a mercenary figure.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “If I can get them with the preservation of my own honor and fidelity and greatness of mind, show me the way and I will get them; but if you require me to lose my own proper good that you may gain what is not good, consider how inequitable and foolish you are.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus refuses any gain that would cost him his integrity.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar’s self-respecting man likewise refuses pleasure that would cost him his good name.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verbatim; strong on protecting one’s own good, though the context is money and office.

kurals.tamil:
நிறைநெஞ்சம் இல்லவர் தோய்வார் பிறநெஞ்சிற்
பேணிப் புணர்பவர் தோள்.
kurals.transliteration:
Nirainenjam illavar thoyvaar piranenjir
penip punarpavar thol.
kurals.meaning: Only those who lack a steady, self-governed heart will seek the arms of women who embrace them while their own hearts are set on something else.
kurals.elementary: Someone who is pretending to be your friend while really thinking about your video games is not giving you their heart. Valluvar says only a person who cannot control their own wishes keeps running after friends like that.
kurals.university: Nirai-nenjam (நிறைநெஞ்சம்) is ‘a full or restrained heart’; nirai is the classical virtue of self-control, the power to hold the mind in check, which Mu. Varadarasanar glosses as ‘the strength to rule one’s heart’. The women are those who embrace while pira-nenjil peni (பிறநெஞ்சிற் பேணி), ‘cherishing something else in their heart’, which Puliyur Kesigan and Solomon Pappaiah identify as the money they want. The couplet thus contrasts two divided states: the women’s hearts are elsewhere, and the men lack a governed heart of their own. Parimelazhagar connects nirai with the self-mastery praised in chapter 13 (Adakkamudaimai). Both base sources agree on the text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Katha Upanishad’s chariot image, the senses are horses and the mind the reins; for one who lacks understanding and whose mind is never held firm, the senses run wild like a charioteer’s vicious horses.
hinduism.explanation: The Upanishad teaches that an unrestrained mind lets the senses drag a person wherever they go.
hinduism.tie_back: Kural 917’s men without nirai-nenjam are exactly such charioteers who have lost the reins.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close on self-control as the dividing line; paraphrased.

christianity.quote_or_event: “He that hath no rule over his own spirit is like a city that is broken down, and without walls.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs compares a person without self-control to a city with no defenses.
christianity.tie_back: Valluvar’s nirai-nenjam illavar are this undefended city.
christianity._accuracy_note: Near-exact match on lack of self-rule.

islam.quote_or_event: “But as for he who feared the position of his Lord and prevented the soul from [unlawful] inclination,” (the next verse adds: then Paradise will be his refuge).
islam.explanation: The Qur’an praises the one who restrains the self from its desires.
islam.tie_back: This is the nirai-nenjam that Kural 917 says the weak lack.
islam._accuracy_note: Verse 40 quoted verbatim; strong match on restraining the self.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Who is mighty? He who subdues his [evil] inclination, as it is said: ‘He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that rules his spirit than he that takes a city’.”
judaism.explanation: Ben Zoma defines true strength as mastery of one’s own impulses.
judaism.tie_back: Kural 917 measures a man the same way: those without that mastery are the ones who fall.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong match on self-mastery as the decisive virtue.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “For a person tormented by evil thoughts, who is passion-dominated and given to the pursuit of pleasure, his craving steadily grows. He makes the fetter strong, indeed.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says an undisciplined mind makes the fetter of craving stronger.
buddhism.tie_back: Valluvar’s men without a governed heart tighten that fetter by seeking such company.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good match on the uncontrolled mind driving pursuit of pleasure.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Circe turns Odysseus’ companions into swine with her enchanted food, but Odysseus, protected by the herb moly from Hermes, keeps his mind and is not changed.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth separates those overcome by enchantment from the one who keeps control of himself.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Kural 917’s nirai-nenjam is Odysseus’ moly: without it, men are transformed by seduction.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good thematic parallel on self-possession versus being overcome; paraphrased.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “If you see an attractive person, you will find that self-restraint is the ability you have against your desire.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus teaches that each temptation calls on a matching inner capacity.
philosophy.tie_back: That capacity is Valluvar’s nirai, and those who lack it are the ones Kural 917 describes.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Direct match on self-restraint as the answer to attraction.

kurals.tamil:
ஆயும் அறிவினர் அல்லார்க்கு அணங்கென்ப
மாய மகளிர் முயக்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Aayum arivinar allaarkku anangenba
maaya magalir muyakku.
kurals.meaning: For those who lack the wisdom to look closely, the embrace of deceitful women is said to be like being seized by an enchanting spirit that leads them to ruin.
kurals.elementary: In fairy tales, a magic song can make people forget who they are and walk into trouble. Valluvar says that people who do not stop to think can be ‘enchanted’ by false affection in the same way, while thoughtful people can see the trick.
kurals.university: Anangu (அணங்கு) in Sangam usage is a dangerous divine power, often a female spirit that seizes and afflicts; Mu. Varadarasanar glosses it as anangu-thaakku, ‘the attack of an anangu’, and as ‘Mohini’s bewitchment’, and Solomon Pappaiah as ‘a deity who stirs desire and takes life’. Maaya magalir (மாய மகளிர்) are women skilled in maayam (மாயம், deception, illusion). The decisive phrase is aayum arivinar allaar (ஆயும் அறிவினர் அல்லார்), ‘those who are not of examining intelligence’: only they experience this as a supernatural seizure, whereas the discerning see an ordinary deception. Enba (என்ப, ‘they say’) marks this as received opinion. Sivayogi Sivakumar alone reads anangu in the positive sense of ‘divine’, as what the foolish mistake such embraces for. Both sources agree on the text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: At the churning of the ocean, Vishnu takes the form of the enchantress Mohini; the asuras, dazzled by her beauty, hand her the pot of amrita to share out, and she gives it to the devas while the asuras are left with nothing.
hinduism.explanation: The Mohini episode shows how enchantment makes the undiscerning give away what matters most.
hinduism.tie_back: Kalaignar and Mu. Varadarasanar themselves gloss Kural 918’s anangu as ‘Mohini mayakkam’, the Mohini bewitchment.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Tamil commentators make this link themselves; Mohini’s deception is divine, not mercenary.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But every man is tempted, when he is drawn away of his own lust, and enticed.”
christianity.explanation: James locates the power of temptation in a person’s own desire.
christianity.tie_back: Valluvar likewise implies that the ‘spirit’ works only on those who do not examine themselves.
christianity._accuracy_note: Matches the idea that enticement grips the unexamined mind.

islam.quote_or_event: “...And what is the worldly life except the enjoyment of delusion.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an calls worldly attractions a pleasure that deceives.
islam.tie_back: Kural 918’s maayam (illusion) is one form of that deceiving enjoyment.
islam._accuracy_note: Shares the concept of delusive pleasure; general rather than specific.

judaism.quote_or_event: Delilah is paid in silver by the Philistine lords to discover the secret of Samson’s strength; she presses him with claims of love until he tells her, and he is captured and blinded.
judaism.explanation: The story is the Hebrew Bible’s classic example of a strong man undone by paid, deceptive affection.
judaism.tie_back: Samson, mighty but undiscerning, is the man of Kural 918 who cannot see through maaya affection.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong narrative match combining money, deception and an undiscerning victim; paraphrased.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Those who are lust-infatuated fall back into the swirling current (of samsara) like a spider on its self-spun web.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says infatuation traps a person in a web of their own making.
buddhism.tie_back: In Kural 918, the ‘spell’ that grips the undiscerning is likewise partly their own doing.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Matches infatuation as a trap; no idea of external deception.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “First you will come to the Sirens who enchant all who come near them. If any one unwarily draws in too close and hears the singing of the Sirens, his wife and children will never welcome him home again...”
greek_mythology.explanation: Circe warns Odysseus that the Sirens’ sweet song draws careless sailors to their death; he survives by having himself bound to the mast.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Sirens are a Greek anangu: fatal only to those who come close ‘unwarily’, without the foresight Valluvar calls aayum arivu.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verbatim from Butler; very close to the image of a deadly enchanting female power.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “If you are struck by the appearance of any promised pleasure, guard yourself against being hurried away by it; but let the affair wait your leisure, and procure yourself some delay.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus advises pausing to examine a tempting impression before acting on it.
philosophy.tie_back: This pause is precisely the aayum arivu (examining intelligence) that Kural 918 says protects against enchantment.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong match: examination as the defense against seductive appearance.

kurals.tamil:
வரைவிலா மாணிழையார் மென்தோள் புரையிலாப்
பூரியர்கள் ஆழும் அளறு.
kurals.transliteration:
Varaivilaa maanizhaiyaar mendhol puraiyilaap
pooriyargal aazhum alaru.
kurals.meaning: The soft arms of jewelled women who keep no limits are a hell-like mire into which base, undiscerning men sink.
kurals.elementary: Picture a pretty field that is really a deep mud bog. It looks soft and inviting, but anyone who walks in without thinking gets stuck and sinks. Valluvar says that ‘love’ that is only bought and sold is like that bog.
kurals.university: This couplet supplies the chapter’s title word: varaivilaa (வரைவிலா), ‘without varaivu’. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses varaivu as ‘a moral limit’ (ozhukka varaiyarai), and Puliyur Kesigan and Solomon Pappaiah as ‘not distinguishing between high and low’ among those who pay; in akam poetry varaivu also means ‘marriage’, which yields the reading ‘women outside wedlock’. Maanizhaiyaar (மாணிழையார்) is ‘those with fine jewels’. Alaru (அளறு) means both mire or mud and naraka (hell), and the commentators exploit both: Kalaignar speaks of ‘the mire called hell’. Puraiyilaa pooriyargal (புரையிலாப் பூரியர்கள்) are ‘base men without worth’; Sivayogi Sivakumar takes purai as ‘fault’, so ‘those who do not know what is wrong’. Both sources agree on the text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “There are three gates leading to the hell of self-destruction for the soul—lust, anger, and greed. Therefore, one should abandon all three.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna names lust and greed among the gates to hell.
hinduism.tie_back: Kural 919 pictures the place where lust on one side and greed on the other meet as alaru, a hell-mire.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong match on lust and greed as the gateway to a hell-like ruin.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Her feet go down to death; her steps take hold on hell.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs describes the path of the ‘strange woman’ as leading down to death and hell.
christianity.tie_back: Valluvar’s alaru is the same downward destination.
christianity._accuracy_note: Very close: both call such intimacy a road to hell.

islam.quote_or_event: The Qur’an tells believers not even to come near zina (unlawful intimacy), calling it a shameful deed and an evil way.
islam.explanation: The command is to keep clear of the path altogether, not merely to avoid the final act.
islam.tie_back: Kural 919 likewise treats the path itself as a mire that swallows those who enter.
islam._accuracy_note: Close on avoidance of the whole path; paraphrased for an all-ages readership.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A prostitute is a deep pit; A forbidden woman is a narrow well.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs compares such company to a deep pit that is hard to climb out of.
judaism.tie_back: Almost the same image as Valluvar’s alaru, the mire in which base men sink.
judaism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match: pit or well versus mire.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Whoever is overcome by this wretched and sticky craving, his sorrows grow like grass after the rains.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada calls craving ‘sticky’, something that clings and spreads sorrow.
buddhism.tie_back: Valluvar’s mire is also sticky: those who step in sink further.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Shared ‘sticky trap’ imagery; the Dhammapada speaks of craving in general.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Odysseus’ scouts in the land of the Lotus-Eaters taste the honey-sweet lotus and lose all wish to return home; he has to drag them back to the ships by force.
greek_mythology.explanation: The episode shows pleasure that makes people forget their purpose and stay stuck.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Kural 919’s base men likewise sink into a sweet-seeming mire they cannot leave.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Loose parallel of being stuck in pleasure; the lotus has nothing to do with mercenary love.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “...he who passes unsanctified and uninitiated into the world below will live in a slough, but that he who arrives there after initiation and purification will dwell with the gods.”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates cites the mystery teaching that the impure soul ends in a slough, a muddy swamp, in the afterlife.
philosophy.tie_back: Plato’s slough and Valluvar’s alaru are the same image: an unpurified life sinks into mire.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verbatim; strong match on the mire-as-hell image, though Plato speaks of impurity in general.

kurals.tamil:
இருமனப் பெண்டிரும் கள்ளும் கவறும்
திருநீக்கப் பட்டார் தொடர்பு.
kurals.transliteration:
Irumanap pendirum kallum kavarum
thiruneekkap pattaar thodarbu.
kurals.meaning: Double-minded women, strong drink and gambling dice are the companions of those whom good fortune has abandoned.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a kid who spends all their allowance on silly gambling games at the fair, sugary junk, and ‘friends’ who only like them for their money. Soon the money is gone and so are the ‘friends’. Valluvar says these habits are a sign that someone’s good luck is slipping away.
kurals.university: The closing couplet groups three ruinous attachments: irumanap pendir (இருமனப் பெண்டிர், ‘women of two minds’, whose heart is in one place and body in another, as Solomon Pappaiah explains), kal (கள், toddy or liquor) and kavaru (கவறு, dice). Their thodarbu (தொடர்பு, ‘association’) belongs to those thiru-neekkap-pattaar (திருநீக்கப் பட்டார்), ‘those from whom Thiru has been removed’; Thiru is both fortune and the goddess Lakshmi (Thirumagal), which is how Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesigan read it. Parimelazhagar notes that the couplet links this chapter to the next two, Kallunnaamai (93, not drinking) and Soodhu (94, gambling), so it works as a hinge for the whole cluster of vices. Both sources agree on the text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Drinking, dice, women, and hunting, these four (which have been enumerated) in succession, he must know to be the most pernicious in the set that springs from love of pleasure.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu warns a king that these are the worst of the vices born of love of pleasure.
hinduism.tie_back: Three of Manu’s four (drink, dice, women) are exactly Valluvar’s triad of ruin.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match on the triad and on its ruinous effect.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And not many days after the younger son gathered all together, and took his journey into a far country, and there wasted his substance with riotous living.”
christianity.explanation: The Prodigal Son loses his inheritance through careless living; his brother later accuses him of spending it on harlots (Luke 15:30).
christianity.tie_back: The prodigal is the thiru-neekkap-pattaan, the man whose fortune leaves him through such company.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong narrative match on fortune lost to dissipation; dice are not mentioned.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, indeed, intoxicants, gambling, [sacrificing on] stone alters [to other than Allah], and divining arrows are but defilement from the work of Satan, so avoid it that you may be successful.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an groups intoxicants and gambling as works of Satan to be avoided for success.
islam.tie_back: Two of Valluvar’s three ruinous companions appear here, set against ‘success’ (falah), close to Valluvar’s thiru.
islam._accuracy_note: Close match on drink and gambling; women are not in this verse.

judaism.quote_or_event: “He that loveth pleasure shall be a poor man; He that loveth wine and oil shall not be rich.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs links the love of pleasure and wine to poverty.
judaism.tie_back: Valluvar likewise says such loves are the company of those whom fortune has left.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good match on pleasure and wine causing loss of fortune; dice are absent.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Dice, women, liquor, dancing, singing, sleeping by day, sauntering at unseemly hours, evil companions, avarice — these nine causes ruin a man.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists, among causes of ruin, the very triad Valluvar names.
buddhism.tie_back: Dice, women, liquor appear at the head of the list, mirroring Kural 920’s triad of lost fortune.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near-exact match on the triad and on ruin.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Elpenor, the youngest of Odysseus’ crew, drinks heavily in Circe’s house, sleeps on the roof, and in the morning stumbles off it and breaks his neck.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer’s small tragedy shows indulgence bringing sudden, pointless ruin.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Elpenor is a minor Greek example of the drink in Kural 920’s triad of misfortune.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Covers only drink, and Elpenor is foolish rather than abandoned by fortune.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epicurus writes that a pleasant life is produced not by continuous drinking and revelry, nor by sensual indulgence or luxurious tables, but by sober reasoning that examines every choice and avoidance.
philosophy.explanation: Even the philosopher of pleasure rejects drinking, revelry and indulgence as the path to happiness.
philosophy.tie_back: Kural 920’s ruinous companions are the very things Epicurus says do not make life good.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased from the standard Hicks translation, not re-checked live; good match on drink and indulgence, no mention of gambling.
